cards.definition: The ancient Greek theory that the body contained four fluids — blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile — and that illness was caused by an imbalance of these.
The belief that disease was caused by breathing in 'bad air' from rotting matter; widely accepted in the medieval period.
A Roman physician whose ideas about anatomy and the four humours dominated medical thinking for over 1,000 years.
Ancient Greek doctor known as the 'Father of Medicine' who promoted observation of symptoms and natural rather than supernatural causes of disease.
A common medieval treatment involving removing blood from the patient to restore the balance of humours.
A medieval tradesperson who made and sold herbal remedies and medicines.
A trained, university-educated doctor in the medieval period who diagnosed illness using theory rather than surgery.
A practitioner in the medieval period who performed practical procedures such as tooth-pulling, wound dressing and amputation.
The devastating plague of 1348–49 that killed around a third of England's population; its cause was not understood and responses were ineffective.
The belief that illness was caused by God as a punishment for sin, or by the influence of planets and astrology.
16th-century Flemish anatomist who proved Galen wrong by dissecting human corpses and publishing accurate anatomical drawings in 'On the Fabric of the Human Body' (1543).
English physician who proved in 1628 that blood circulates around the body, pumped by the heart, overturning Galen's theory.
17th-century doctor who promoted careful observation and recording of symptoms to identify and categorise diseases.
French surgeon who improved wound treatment by using ligatures to tie blood vessels instead of cauterisation, and developed prosthetic limbs.
Gutenberg's invention (c.1440) that allowed medical ideas and anatomical illustrations to spread rapidly across Europe.
The cutting open and examination of a dead body to study anatomy; became increasingly acceptable and important in Renaissance medicine.
The 1665 outbreak of bubonic plague in London that killed around 100,000 people; responses remained limited as the cause was still unknown.
A thread used to tie off a blood vessel during surgery to prevent bleeding, introduced by Paré as an alternative to cauterisation.
The medieval practice of sealing wounds by burning them with hot irons to stop bleeding; painful and often fatal.
A scientific institution founded in 1660 that encouraged the sharing of new discoveries and experimental evidence.
English doctor who developed the world's first vaccine in 1796, using cowpox to protect against the deadly disease smallpox.
The introduction of a weakened or related pathogen into the body to stimulate immunity against a disease.
French scientist who proved in the 1850s–60s that microbes (germs) cause disease, establishing Germ Theory.
The scientific understanding, proven by Pasteur and Koch, that specific microorganisms cause specific diseases.
German scientist who identified the specific bacteria causing tuberculosis (1882) and cholera (1883), advancing Germ Theory.
A doctor who traced the 1854 Soho cholera outbreak to a contaminated water pump, providing key evidence against miasma theory.
A waterborne disease that caused major epidemics in 19th-century Britain, driving improvements in public health and sanitation.
Legislation that compelled local councils to provide clean water, sewers, street lighting and refuse collection across Britain.
Surgeon who introduced antiseptic carbolic acid spray into operating theatres in the 1860s, dramatically reducing post-operative infection.
A substance that removes sensation or consciousness during surgery; ether and chloroform were introduced in the 1840s.
Scottish scientist who discovered in 1928 that the Penicillium mould killed bacteria, leading to the development of penicillin.
The world's first antibiotic, developed by Florey and Chain from Fleming's discovery and mass-produced from 1943 onwards.
A medicine that kills or inhibits the growth of bacteria, revolutionising the treatment of previously fatal infections.
A controlled experiment testing a new treatment on human patients to assess its safety and effectiveness before widespread use.
The structure of DNA, discovered by Watson and Crick in 1953, opening the way for genetic medicine and understanding hereditary disease.
Founded in 1948 by Aneurin Bevan, providing free healthcare for all at the point of use, funded through taxation.
A behaviour or habit — such as smoking, diet or exercise — that increases or decreases a person's risk of disease.
In the 1950s, Doll and Hill proved the statistical link between smoking tobacco and lung cancer, eventually leading to public health campaigns.
A term used by Paul Ehrlich to describe a chemical that targets a specific pathogen without harming the patient; Salvarsan 606 (1909) was the first.
A government-organised schedule of vaccines given to children to prevent the spread of infectious diseases across the population.
The system of defensive trenches used in World War One that caused specific injury patterns, including shrapnel wounds, gas injuries and trench foot.
A psychological condition caused by the trauma of warfare, characterised by tremors, anxiety and mental breakdown; poorly understood at the time.
Women's voluntary organisation that drove ambulances and staffed field hospitals on the Western Front.
The process of sorting casualties by the severity of their wounds to prioritise treatment and make the best use of medical resources.
A medical facility located just behind the front line where soldiers received more advanced treatment before being evacuated further.
The transfer of blood from a donor to a patient; refrigerated blood banks developed during WWI made this practical for the first time.
Used in WWI field hospitals to locate bullets and shrapnel inside the body; Marie Curie helped equip mobile X-ray units.
Antiseptic kills germs with chemicals; aseptic surgery prevents germs entering the wound through sterile conditions — both developed in WWI hospitals.
Reconstructive surgery to repair facial and other injuries; pioneered by Harold Gillies at Sidcup during WWI.
A deadly bacterial infection of wounds that thrived in the muddy, contaminated conditions of the trenches and was extremely difficult to treat.
Queen of England from 1558 to 1603; navigated religious division, foreign threats and court politics to establish a stable reign.
The monarch's advisory body of senior councillors who helped govern England; Elizabeth used it to balance different factions.
Elizabeth's compromise that made England Protestant again, establishing the Church of England with the monarch as Supreme Governor.
Restored royal control over the Church of England, making Elizabeth Supreme Governor rather than Supreme Head.
Required all churches to use the Protestant Book of Common Prayer and all people to attend church on Sundays.
A Protestant who wanted to 'purify' the Church of England of all remaining Catholic elements and ceremonies.
The danger posed to Elizabeth by Catholics at home and abroad who believed Mary Queen of Scots had a stronger claim to the throne.
Catholic cousin of Elizabeth who was a focal point for plots against the queen; held captive from 1568 and executed in 1587.
Pope Pius V's papal bull declaring Elizabeth a heretic and releasing Catholics from loyalty to her, intensifying the Catholic threat.
The body that granted taxes and passed laws; Elizabeth managed it carefully, keeping MPs' interference in policy to a minimum.
Legislation that distinguished between the 'deserving' poor (ill/elderly) and 'idle' poor (able-bodied), providing different responses to poverty.
The act of wandering without work; vagabonds were feared and punished harshly in Elizabethan England as a threat to social order.
The process of landowners fencing off common land, driving many rural workers off the land and contributing to poverty and vagrancy.
A fleet of 130 Spanish ships sent by Philip II to invade England; defeated by a combination of English tactics and storms.
Catholic king of Spain who launched the Armada against England, motivated by religion, politics and England's support for Dutch rebels.
English privateer and naval commander who raided Spanish ports and helped defeat the Armada; second-in-command of the English fleet.
State-approved pirates licensed by Elizabeth to attack Spanish ships and steal treasure, damaging Spanish wealth without open war.
The rebellion of the Protestant Netherlands against Spanish Catholic rule; Elizabeth provided troops and funds, angering Philip II.
Elizabeth's famous speech to troops before the Armada battle, declaring she had 'the heart and stomach of a king', boosting morale.
A symbolic image of Elizabeth as the ideal, glorious queen used in portraits and propaganda to project power and inspire loyalty.

topics.name: Conflict & Tension: The First World War

cards.definition: The four long-term causes of WWI: Militarism, Alliance systems, Imperialism and Nationalism.
A network of agreements between nations that meant a conflict between two countries could rapidly drag in many others.
The alliance between Britain, France and Russia that formed one side of the conflict in WWI.
The pre-war alliance between Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy (though Italy did not fight for them in 1914).
The policy of building up large armed forces and glorifying military power, contributing to an arms race before 1914.
Strong pride in one's nation or ethnic group; in the Balkans it fuelled demands for independence from Austria-Hungary.
The murder of the heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914 by Gavrilo Princip, triggering the July Crisis.
Germany's pre-war strategy to defeat France quickly via Belgium before turning to face Russia, bringing Britain into the war.
The escalating sequence of ultimatums, mobilisations and declarations of war in July–August 1914 that turned the assassination into a world war.
Competition between European powers for overseas colonies and global influence, creating tensions and rivalries before 1914.
The military deadlock on the Western Front where neither side could advance, leading to years of trench warfare.
A major WWI offensive in which British forces suffered 57,000 casualties on the first day; intended to relieve pressure on Verdun.
Compulsory military service introduced in Britain in 1916 when voluntary recruitment was no longer sufficient.
Information designed to promote a particular viewpoint; used by all sides to encourage recruitment and maintain morale.
America joined the Allies in April 1917 after German unrestricted submarine warfare and the Zimmermann Telegram shifted US opinion.
The agreement to stop fighting that ended WWI at 11am on 11 November 1918.
The peace settlement that ended WWI, imposing harsh terms on Germany including reparations, territorial losses and the War Guilt Clause.
The clause in the Treaty of Versailles that forced Germany to accept full blame for starting the war.
Financial compensation Germany was ordered to pay the Allies under the Treaty of Versailles, eventually set at £6.6 billion.
An international organisation established after WWI to resolve disputes peacefully and prevent future wars, but weakened by the USA's absence.
The democratic government established in Germany after WWI in 1919, named after the city where its constitution was written.
The Weimar voting system where parties gained seats in proportion to their share of votes, leading to coalition governments and instability.
A clause in the Weimar Constitution allowing the president to rule by emergency decree without consulting the Reichstag.
A catastrophic rise in prices in Germany in 1923, caused by the government printing money to pay reparations; savings became worthless.
France and Belgium occupied the Ruhr industrial region when Germany defaulted on reparations payments, triggering the economic crisis.
A period of relative stability under Foreign Minister Gustav Stresemann, with economic recovery (Dawes Plan), cultural flourishing and international acceptance.
The collapse of the American stock market in October 1929 that triggered a global depression, causing mass unemployment in Germany.
Hitler's failed attempt to seize power by force in Munich; his subsequent trial gave him national publicity.
An American-backed agreement that restructured German reparations payments and provided US loans to stabilise the German economy.
The German parliament in the Weimar Republic; its inability to form stable majorities weakened democracy.
The National Socialist German Workers' Party, led by Adolf Hitler; rose to power by exploiting economic crisis and political instability.
Austrian-born leader of the Nazi Party who became Chancellor of Germany in January 1933 and established a totalitarian dictatorship.
Controlled information used by the Nazis to spread their ideology; Joseph Goebbels ran the Ministry of Propaganda from 1933.
The Nazi paramilitary force used to intimidate political opponents and protect party meetings during the rise to power.
Law passed after the Reichstag fire that gave Hitler the power to govern by decree for four years, bypassing parliament.
The burning of the German parliament building; the Nazis blamed the Communists and used it to justify emergency powers.
Hitler's purge of SA leaders and political rivals in June 1934, consolidating his power and reassuring the army.
The title meaning 'leader' adopted by Hitler when he merged the roles of Chancellor and President after Hindenburg's death in 1934.
The Nazi secret police, used to monitor, arrest and terrorise political opponents and anyone seen as a threat to the regime.
Hitler's elite personal bodyguard and security organisation, later responsible for running concentration camps.
The Nazi ideal of a 'people's community' — a racially pure, unified German society in which everyone worked for the nation.
The Nazi organisation for boys aged 14–18 that trained them in military skills and indoctrinated them in Nazi ideology.
The female equivalent of Hitler Youth, which trained girls to become healthy mothers and homemakers for the Nazi state.
Laws that stripped Jewish people of German citizenship and banned marriage between Jews and non-Jews.
The 'Night of Broken Glass' — a nationwide pogrom on 9–10 November 1938 in which Jewish businesses, synagogues and homes were attacked.
Prison camps where political opponents, Jewish people and others were detained, forced to work or murdered by the Nazi regime.
The systematic genocide of six million Jewish people and millions of others (Roma, disabled people, etc.) by the Nazi regime.
The motorway network built by the Nazis, used as evidence of economic recovery and presented as a symbol of Nazi modernisation.
Germany's rapid build-up of its armed forces from 1933, in secret at first and then openly from 1935, in violation of the Treaty of Versailles.
Resistance to the Nazi regime, including the White Rose group, Swing Youth and individuals such as Dietrich Bonhoeffer, was rare and dangerous.
